text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on January 21 in history.

1769 - The mysterious Letters of Junius began appearing in the London Public Advertiser. Commenting on, and warning about, public affairs and personalities, the author of them was never definitely established.
1793 - King Louis XVI of France was guillotined for treason. He had ruled since 1774 and had remained King for three years after the Revolution of 1789.

1824 - Thomas Jonathan "Stonewall' Jackson, U.S. confederate general, born. After repulsing Joseph Hooker at Chancellorsville, Jackson's reconnaissance party was accidentally fired on by his own troops and he died soon after.
1829 - Oscar II, king of Norway and Sweden, born. Unable to maintain the union of Norway and Sweden, he surrendered the former crown to Prince Carl of Denmark.
1899 - Britain's Lord Kitchener was appointed the Governor- general of Sudan.
1901 - Elisha Gray, U.S. inventor who contested the first patent for the telephone with Alexander Graham Bell, died.
1905 - Christian Dior, French fashion designer who helped revolutionise clothing after World War Two, born.
1911 - The first Monte Carlo motor rally began.
1924 - Soviet leader Lenin died of a brain haemorrhage. He had led the Bolsheviks to victory in the 1917 October Revolution and in its aftermath, had grappled with anarchy and war.
1932 - Lytton Giles Strachey, British biographer, critic and member of the Bloomsbury Group, died.
1941 - Placido Domingo, Spanish operatic tenor, born. One of the world's leading lyric-dramatic tenors, he trained at the National Conservatory of Music, Mexico City.
1942 - German forces under Erwin Rommell launched a counter-offensive in North Africa. Caught by surprise, the British were forced into a retreat across the desert.
1950 - George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair), Indian-born British novelist and essayist, notably of "Animal Farm" and "Nineteen Eighty-four", died.
1954 - Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered submarine, was launched.
1959 - Cecil B(lount) de Mille, U.S. film director and screenwriter, died. His reputation was based on vast film spectaculars, such as "The Ten Commandments".
1965 - Hassan Ali Mansur, Prime Minister of Persia, was assassinated.
1976 - Two Concorde aircraft entered service simultaneously with flights from London to Bahrain and Paris to Rio de Janeiro. These were the first scheduled passenger services by supersonic aircraft.
1976 - Western newspapers, including the Financial Times and New York Times went on sale in the Soviet Union for the first time.
1980 - An Iran Air Boeing 727 flying from Mashad to Tehran crashed on a mountainside in fog, killing all 128 on board.
1984 - Britain's first test-tube triplets - a girl and two boys - born to a couple in London. The mother was Anne Maaye.
1990 - East German Communist party expelled former leader Egon Krenz and 13 other politburo members.
1994 - Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Guy Coeme and two other leading Socialist politicians resigned over a bribery scandal.
